utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you have something to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have a motion that hopefully the Trial Chamber has received this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I've seen this briefly, and it comes -- if it deals with evidence we've already heard, then it -- in its current formulation it comes too late.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to bar any evidence that the Prosecution might lead. I have no way of knowing what they intend to lead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What you'll have to do now is in the event something emerges, raise the matter at that stage, and we will address the issue in the context of the trial. We're not revisiting evidence which has already been led in the case without taking objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did object and it became as a complete surprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When did you object?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, we objected to the question that was raised where the Prosecution directly tried to bring in the police and implied that it was the VJ and the police, when all the witnesses say it was the VJ and Arkan's men. At line 24 and 25 of page 9126, the question was raised: "And was this only VJ soldiers in this group you call infantry or were there also police" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That was an objection to a leading question, it wasn't an objection to any reference to the police. Please, don't mislead us. There was no objection taken to evidence being led about the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Because we had to verify the disclosure. It came as a shock to us that they could be asking so many questions about the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You should have taken the point at that stage that this was not something covered by the Rule 65 ter summary as you're now contending. If in some reason you're prejudiced by this, then your remedy is not the one you're now seeking. Your remedy is a different remedy. If you address that if it arises, then we will address it. Equally, if you contend that a later question asked by the Prosecution causes a problem, then we will address the issue at that stage, but we're not going to start -- this is a matter of principle. We are not going to start revisiting evidence on the basis of objections not raised at the time. We'll be hear forever if we do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree, but I'm also trying, Your Honour, to forestall any practice that appears to be developing on the part of the Prosecution to be making last-minute changes and bringing every witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You know there's sympathy to that, but it has to be raised at the right time and in the right context. If this causes you some sort of prejudice other than being evidence against you that's meant to be prejudicial anyway, if it causes you some unfair evidence, then it's for you to raise that with us and we'll address that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That will be, for example, by adjourning or whatever. But now that evidence is before us, then we have to deal with it and make sure you have a fair opportunity to deal with it, too. If, as I repeat, the issue arises again, we will address it if you take an objection at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Meanwhile we intend to continue with the witness's evidence. Can we please bring the witness in. We need to go into closed session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I should alert you, Ms. Moeller, to two difficulties that I have about the evidence we heard yesterday. I cannot find on my atlas a place called Smolice -- Smolnica, rather. I can find Smolice, but I can't find Smolnica. And, secondly, it wasn't clear to me what dates we were dealing with when we heard evidence about the killing by the person called Zemunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to clear that up today. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yesterday, we left off when you were telling the Trial Chamber about the killing in which this person nicknamed Zemunac was involved. Can you tell the Court when this killing approximately happened, when did you observe that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was when we were in the villages around Orahovac, after the 24th of March, after the NATO air-strikes had begun.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And do you know in which month it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: March, but after the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm now referring to the killing incident itself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in late March, maybe after some ten days of having been in the villages around Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And just to clarify, again, how long altogether did you stay in the Orahovac area and participate in searches, as you described yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Asked and answered, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the answer, Mr. Lukic? 20 to 23 days?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'll move on then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yesterday, Judge Bonomy asked you whether you saw killings happen only on this one occasion or on any others, and you said that: "I didn't see that happening, that they would wear these uniforms, put them on and be killed, but another time I saw a group who were killed." Can you explain what you meant by that because it is a bit unclear.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't see them being killed, or being dressed, uh... I saw another group of people who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when, approximately, was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Do you mean when was it that I saw this other group?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the other group as we were retreating from, uh, when we were at Zub by the ambush, when we were on patrol -actually it wasn’t our patrol but, uh, another patrol, and that’s where I saw eight people, eight victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when were you at Zub, during which period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We returned sometime in April, around the 10th or the 12th of April of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And by "returned," you mean going -- returning where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We returned from the villages around Orahovac to our positions at Zub.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And then how long did you stay at Zub?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the way to the end when there was an agreement reached and a truce announced between the armies when something had been signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Do you know which month that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the agreement was in June. In June, we returned from there to Leskovac. At Medvedja and Medani, we were at a certain school.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. These eight bodies, were they men or women?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were men and then elderly women. Everyone else was male.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what happened to them. It is said that they encountered some VJ soldiers, that they met a regular patrol, and that they refused to stop. After that, they were shot, but I don't know the exact reason why they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how did you come to know this background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We learned that from our superior, from a commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A moment ago you said there was an ambush and a patrol was attacked, and then there were eight bodies. Now, was there an ambush of the patrol -- of the Serb patrol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, why did you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the Army of Yugoslavia was patrolling there and that they set up an ambush, but it wasn't our unit that was there, the 120 mortar unit. We were around Zub. We set up an ambush there, and that patrol was somewhere else. And they came across another patrol, not our patrol, but the Army of Yugoslavia patrol who had been there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that passage certainly needs to be revisited by the translation unit and the position clarified, because it gives the impression of an attack upon the VJ patrol. So, Mr. Haider, would you arrange for that to be obtained. Since I can't work LiveNote this morning, I can't go back to the exact page reference, but it's part of -- it may be the end of page 5 going into page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's page 5, line 15, the particular paragraph you're referring to; and also just above that, page 5, line 3, there's an indication that they were wearing KLA uniforms but he didn't see them put on them. So it is very confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. So that whole passage on -- the whole of page 15 [sic] needs to be translated for us again, and the recording of the witness's actual words revisited and translated. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Did you receive any orders from commanding officers with regard to these eight bodies?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: ambush or that patrol and to put them on trucks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Witness, from here on when I ask you about commanding officers, could you not mention their names before I explicitly ask you to name the name, please. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever receive any further orders with regard to other bodies in the field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And which were these orders? And don't say who gave them at this point.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: What were you ordered to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was when we were in the surroundings of the village of Orahovac. There we were given an order that two soldiers go to report to a superior there. Some bodies were supposed to be loaded on to trucks, some of them were in plastic bags, some were without, and they wore civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how many bodies are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, around 20. When I arrived there, some of the bodies had already been loaded on to trucks. There were around 20. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what happened to the bodies then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were put on the trucks, and there was an armoured vehicle and there was seven or eight of us in that vehicle. We secured and escorted the truck all the way to the power-plant at Obilic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And where is that, Obilic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I think it is -- it comes after Pristina. I don't know exactly. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the connection between the eight bodies you mentioned a little while ago at the ambush and the 20 bodies that we now have in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no connection between the 20 and the eight. I don't know whether they were also transported there. I know about these 20. I don't know about the eight bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So these are all other bodies, as was posed in Ms. Moeller's question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And at the power-plant at Obilic, what happened to the bodies there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. We unloaded them in front of the power-plant. There was some soldiers there and civilians. I don't know whether they were employees of the plant. In any case, I don't know what they did with the bodies. We left them there and returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for one question that may help identify the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. With regard to the searches in the Orahovac area we talked about yesterday, did you see any burning of houses during these searches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were houses burning, but they were not destroyed totally. They were just burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did you see how it came about that they were burning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Were you ever --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I see Mr. Cepic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If you allow me to say, I think that in this translation about previous sentence of which witness said I think that something is missing, just couple words, probably one or two words. If I can translate, he testified that he saw just a couple houses, that they were burning, so it is a little bit different than in the transcript. This is line 21, page 10 -- 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Witness, when you were referring to seeing houses burning, did you say anything about the number of houses you saw burning?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller, you might wish to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You said, yesterday, you went through a couple of villages during these searches. In how many villages did you see houses burning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly in how many villages. Well, houses were not burning in each and every village. It was here and there; then we would be told there was a lot of ammunition found at that house or it was used by the KLA, and that's why it was set on fire. There was no arson just like that, but there was always some justification that there were uniforms there or that those houses were used as shelters or quarters, and that's why they were burned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And who told you about these justifications? And don't say any names, but just, generally, who would tell you about these justifications, as you call them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what we were told by the commander of the 1st Platoon, who was our superior officer in the 1st Platoon. He told us that this had been the reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Were you, yourself, ever ordered to burn a house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was on one occasion, but this was not in the vicinity of Orahovac, but some ten days before we withdrew from Kosovo in Zub.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I would like to go into private session for the details for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: During your time in Orahovac or later in Zub, did you notice any looting going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what was looted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what they took from the houses, what] They put in their pockets, but I know that they took tractors, cars, trucks. That's what I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And where did you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we withdrew our unit in the vicinity of Orahovac, there were some civilian cars because the licence plates were not those of the Yugoslav Army but the civilian licence plates, Orahovac, Djakovica licence plates. So it's possible that those cars were the property of some of the officers, but at any rate they went with us as we withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Who was driving these cars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know because the soldiers couldn't see [as interpreted] that. We were always on trucks. It's possible that those were soldiers, but it is unlikely. I assume that these would be our commanding officers, our superiors.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when you -- when the units withdrew from Kosovo in June --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, but I think we have again problem in transcript. Line 21, I think that the witness said: Because the soldiers couldn't "do" that, not "see" that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It makes sense certainly. Witness, you were asked who was driving the cars, and you said it was -- you assumed it would be commanding officers, but just before that you said: "I don't know because the soldiers couldn't" something, "we were always on trucks." Now, did you say the soldiers couldn't do that or couldn't see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It couldn't have been the soldiers because these soldiers were not allowed to drive cars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I started asking you when you withdrew from Kosovo with the unit in June 1999. Did you see any of these vehicles withdrawing out of Kosovo with the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what kind of cars would that be mainly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Golf, Mercedes, not a Zastava car, newer vehicles, more valuable vehicles, Golf, Mercedes, that type of vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Witness K89, yesterday, when asked about killings, you testified that there would be columns of refugees. Apart from the one incident we talked about yesterday where men were separated from such a column and killed, did you see any other refugee columns in 1999 while you were in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And where did you see such column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw the columns afterwards when we were at Zub, because on the road that they took we saw the columns. There was a large column, mostly women, children, the elderly, the infirm. So that was the road leading to Deva. That's where they passed through.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And in which direction was this column heading?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were heading towards the border, towards Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And from which direction was it coming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether they started from the villages or from Djakovica, but at any point -- at any rate they were heading towards our positions at Zub, and then Deva, and then further on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And were there any VJ units around when this convoy passed by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were units, infantry units there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: What, if anything, did they do when the convoy came by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see anyone being killed. I saw them tear up the documents of those who had their IDs. They didn't kill anyone, and they would put the old ones, the infirm ones, on to the trucks and I think they transported them all the way -- almost all the way up to the border with Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And the people that you saw tearing up the ID documents, what uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the uniforms of the Yugoslav Army, camouflage ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now I would like to call up Exhibit P615, page 21, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Witness K89, we are now calling up a map of Kosovo, and I would like you to have a look at a certain area on this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. Could we zoom in a little bit on the upper right-hand side and go down -- no, go a little bit further. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Witness, do you see this map on your screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I would like you to have a look whether you can see some of the villages that you mention in your testimony there; the village of Zub, can you see that on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can the usher maybe hand him a pen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you make a circle around Zub right on the screen, please, with the pen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Right. Now, can you also see Deva on this map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you also mark Deva, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, do you see on this map the village that you called Smolnica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But it doesn't say "Smolnica," it says "Smolice." That's not the way I had said it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you mark the village on the map as the one you thought you were talking about in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And in relation to where Deva and Zub are positioned, would that be the right geographical area where Smolice, as you called it, would have been.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Was it addressed to me?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, Witness. I will repeat it and try to be a bit clearer. The distance between Deva, Zub, and the village you marked as Smolnica, would that be approximately the distance you experienced when you moved between the villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably yes. Yeah, it should be right. I'm not sure, but I think that it should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I can't take this any further here. Could we take an IC shot of this exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be ID115, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And that would also be the end of my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you complete it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is page 22 the page that would show Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, and it is also the page that shows Djakovica. It's unfortunate that we can't have Djakovica and these villages on one page in this atlas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, can we have page 22 now, please. And can we just have it a bit bigger. No, no. We need to have Orahovac more or less in the centre. Slightly bigger. Now, looking at that map, Witness K89, can you see there or point out there - in other words, mark with your pen there - the villages or the area where the villages were that you were in around Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot mark the villages, but they were here in the -- on the left-hand side, that's where the villages were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I want to know. Mark the area in which you were in around Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Unless you actually draw on the map, I can't see what you're -- the area you're marking. If you could take a circle around the area roughly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know whether this was the village, but I think we were here on the left-hand side, those villages around here. I don't know whether this was the exact village, but that would be the rough location where we were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we also take an IC shot of this, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be IC116, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The order, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour: General Lazarevic, General Ojdanic, General Pavkovic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Milutinovic, and General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give me a moment. The cross-examination should take us until -- we should certainly be able to complete it before lunchtime, and it might be a bit earlier than that if we were applying a strict -- involving ourselves in a strict application of the guidelines we've given. So let's make that the outside target for this cross-examination. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness K89, could you please turn in my direction. I would like to introduce myself to you. My name is Djuro Cepic. I'm one of the Defence attorneys representing General Lazarevic. I will be asking you several questions, and I would like to answer as clearly as possible to my questions. And the questions that I will be requesting, I will strive to make them as clear as possible and I would appreciate if you could give me very clear and precise answers, preferably in the form of yes or no. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You arrived in the barracks in Valjevo on the 18th of March, together with all the other recruits; and in the first few weeks before taking your oath and before being issued with a weapon, you take part in some of the basic training where you learn about the basic rights and obligations of the soldiers and all the other rights and obligations that stem from our obligation to do the national service. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not all of them. What we were told -- we were taught first about the use of the rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Witness, before taking the oath, you could not have been issued with a weapon at all. You could not have been taught how to clean the rifle. I'm asking you about the period before you took the oath. You and all the other soldiers had training in the classroom about the basic rights and obligations and basic legal regulations pertaining to the national service. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Witness K89, thousands of soldiers had gone through the barracks there, and they all underwent this training. How come that you are the only one that never underwent this kind of training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did undergo some training, but not about our conduct but we had training that pertained --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had training that pertained -- we were taught about ranks but not conduct. Ranks, we were taught about rifles, various parts. But I did not have any training as to my conduct in war, how to treat the prisoners, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: After that you took your oath. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You were issued a weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have a little pause between question and answer interpreters ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, we're into the constant problem of speaking immediately when the witness finishes. Please allow time for the interpretation to catch up. I think you can now carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You spent two and a half months in training, in fact two months and 20 days, and then a new generation of recruits arrive. The soldiers from your generation received transfers and they're transferred all over the -- Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And then sometime on the 8th of June, you are in Kosovo in the Djakovica barracks. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know exactly whether this was June or late May. That's something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go into private session just for a very brief period of time? I have to ask a question that might be taken in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Hold on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Witness, in Djakovica, you were given your assignment, your uniform, your weapon, and you were given the exact information as to what unit you would be assigned to. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So you went to the camping area of your unit. You said this was in the village of Sulani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to ask the usher to bring to the screen the Exhibit IC115. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Witness K89, could you please show me on this map the village of Sulani.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What would you tell me if I were to put it to you that the village of Sulani does not exist at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Perhaps it's a mountain because there were a couple of villages there. It's possible that such a village does not exist, but the position where we were was called Sulani. And I simply assumed that the village that was below our position was called Sulani.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness K89, do you hold a driver's licence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: When did you get your driver's licence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And you have a driver's licence only for cars. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, for trucks, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So you got it a couple of months ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me go back to your national service in Valjevo. The soldiers in your generation and you yourself, you did go out into town regularly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It was once a week?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were in this base camp area, do you know that in this period when you arrived there, that a soldier was killed in the vicinity of that area, but he belonged to another Yugoslav Army unit and a major was wounded and two other soldiers were wounded in fact. This all happened in the vicinity of the village of Smolice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know about that. I did know that a soldier had been wounded by a mortar shell. It's possible what you're saying, but I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It was a KLA mortar shell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I never asked questions about it, whether it was our shell or a KLA shell. I can only presume that it was fired by the KLA. He couldn't have hurt himself on -- or with his own shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you also know that in June when you arrived at the base camp area, in the area of nearby border post called --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In the area of the nearby border post.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: -- a large group of terrorists attempted to cross the border with a large amount of weaponry and that there was an exchange of fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: For clarification, your unit was undergoing regular training there, as well as securing the state border?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And you underwent regular training there on how to handle mortars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not regular training but the use of mortars. The mortars were at their positions, and we were told how to use the sights to measure distances and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Witness K89, yesterday you testified and described that in -- on the morning of the 25th of March, 1999, with your mortar company headed by your commander, you went towards Orahovac. Your unit set out after the infantry unit because your mortar unit was supposed to support the infantry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And you moved on trucks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And you had your mortars hooked up to the trucks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Throughout your stay in the environs of Orahovac, you didn't use the mortars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When executing assignments in the area of Orahovac, you slept in those or on those trucks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your company commander would not allow you to sleep in the houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your commander was tough, strict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: As regards searches of houses, once completed your company commander would search the soldiers so as to be sure that no one had stolen anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your commander acquainted the soldiers of your unit with the fact that they were not allowed to conduct themselves improperly or steal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in some other cases of other units -- did you know that in some other units any soldiers were found having been stolen anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of anyone stealing anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in your battalion there were over 20 criminal reports submitted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your unit during that assignment moved some two to three kilometres behind the infantry, as was prescribed by the rules on establishment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were closer to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was it one and a half to two kilometres, pursuant to the Rules of Service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was much closer, not one or two kilometres, but perhaps 100 or 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If it was only 100 to 200 metres, you cannot execute your assignment. What you said is illogical. Do you agree with me that it doesn't make sense?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps according to the law and the rules we were supposed to do that, but there was no need for us to be further away. Perhaps there was no need for us to open fire; that's why we were close.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we can conclude that there was no firing, no action?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness K89, before this Chamber there was another witness, a member of the police. He stated that the army in that area never entered villages. Do you agree with his statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: As you stated yesterday, you stayed on that assignment for some 22 or 23 days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: When you saw the person with the nickname of Zemunac firing at some men, as you stated, that was in mid-April. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You don't know where it was. All you know is that it was in mid-April. You actually observed that from a distance of several hundred metres. Am I correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a hundred. Perhaps less. One could see it well. It may have been 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This Zemunac person, as you call him, carried KLA uniforms with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He wore a VJ uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I didn't mean on him, but with him. He had those uniforms.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether he had them in his hands -- I don't think he could carry so many uniforms. They were probably on a truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You didn't see where the uniforms were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You didn't see them put those uniforms on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them take the clothes off them and put the uniforms on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement that I mentioned a while ago, in paragraph 28, you described this incident but you did not specify the unit that had actually done that. You said that this had been done by a group that was involved in the search. You didn't mention any perpetrator. You didn't even mention any nicknames. Can you comment on this statement that I just made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who was the leader of this group. But this man that I knew as Zemunac, he was in the infantry. Now, whether there was a commanding officer there or not who had issued them orders to do that, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How come in your statement you don't mention this nickname Zemunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How come you did not mention this nickname Zemunac in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did. I think I did mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Let me read your statement in the paragraph 28 of your statement. "I saw other groups involved in the searches that would separate the men from the women and children and shoot the men. If they were wearing civilian clothes, they would dress them in KLA uniforms. I do not know where they got those uniforms from, but they were like green camouflage jackets with the red KLA -- UCK patch on the arm. I saw one man making a video recording of how the soldiers were dressing the bodies in the UCK uniforms. I thought to shoot him but I did not and he ran away." This is your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No mention is made of Zemunac, Witness K89?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that at that time I was not asked who did the killing. Had they asked me that, I would probably have included or mentioned this, but nobody had asked me. This is why this is not contained in the statement that I did not mention the man named Zemunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You go on to say in your statement that the next paragraph, 29 --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher to put document 3D496 on the screen. This is the statement that I quoted a little while ago. Could we zoom in on paragraph 29.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, is that in open session now and on the open screen? I would not want it published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It apparently can only be seen in the courtroom, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you see in front of you on the screen your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the statement, but I don't understand the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher to show the witness his version of the statement in B/C/S, or perhaps I could just give my hard copy to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I gather it's not in the system in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will just give him my statement in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bodies that were in the vicinity of Orahovac that you had just described to us, you loaded them on to trucks and you took them to Obilic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps it is not quite clear. This was not done twice because once -- in fact, twice I loaded the bodies; once I went all the way to Obilici, and the second time I just loaded the bodies on to the trucks and I didn't go all the way to Obilici.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So you loaded the bodies with the KLA insignia on to the trucks. You drove them to Obilic. And as you state here, you drove the truck on those two occasions to Obilic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a misunderstanding. We, the soldiers, not I personally. I did not personally drive the truck. We, the soldiers, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can I be clear about one other thing. Did -- or were any of these bodies wearing KLA uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat his answer; it was unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That answer was not heard by the interpreter. Could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the bodies that I loaded, none of them had the uniforms. I don't know whether the bodies that were in the plastic bags, whether they had uniforms on. But the bodies that I saw, they did -- none of them had the KLA uniform on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your question assumed that, I think, Mr. Cepic, but there's been no evidence so far that these bodies that were loaded on to lorries were in KLA uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me, I will try to clarify that. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, after this incident in the location that you cannot specify on the date that you cannot specify, those bodies that remained on the ground were loaded on to trucks by you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So the previous situation that you described, the incident where this man allegedly names Zemunac, this is something you just observed from a distance and nothing else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we observed. We were quite close. I don't know what they did with the bodies. I don't know what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Who observed it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our unit. We did not observe it per se. We were behind them. Our unit was behind them in order to provide support to them. We were in the state of readiness at the stand-by. If anything happened, we were there to give them support. It was not our task to observe anything. We were just standing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So it was your task to give them support from a distance. I mean give support to certain units. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were not told this was our task. We were standing there because they were moving ahead of us, and we stood there to wait. Now, whether we waited for a task to be issued to us, I don't know; but at any rate that's where we were, that's where we were and that's where we remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Witness, is it your testimony today that your unit was moving immediately behind the infantry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So you're saying something that would be contrary to the task, the objective, and the logic, the very logic, of the engagement of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the situation is, how this situation should be handled in peacetime, but I know that we were in wartime. That's how we did that. Perhaps if it had been in peacetime, we would probably have held some distance in accordance with the Rules of Service. But this was a state of war and this is how we did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to the drives to Obilic. In this paragraph of your statement that I quoted, that would be paragraph 29, you say the following. "On at least two occasions, I assisted loading the bodies of the men who were shot on to military lorries and I drove them to the power station behind Pristina called Obilic." So you drove the trucks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, this has been asked and answered twice already. The witness has made it clear what he did. It's not consistent with the statement and that's something you can say later, but you can't keep going over the same ground in the circumstances where, in fact, I've overestimated the time you ought to take for this cross-examination. And it should actually finish half an hour before the lunchtime session finishes, so bear that in mind and try and concentrate on new questions rather than over the same territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I understood. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were executing this task sometime from mid-April and then you went back to Zub?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: All those incidents that occurred, that you described, they happened in mid-April. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the incidents that I saw in the vicinity of Orahovac, they were in mid-April or late April, that would be the rough time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have Defence document 5D87 on our screens. Could we zoom in on paragraph 11, please. Could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Pages9179-9183 redacted. Private session

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we please wait until the curtains are up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Witness K89, we are on the topic of tearing up of documents. You said that you saw that on the road to Deva?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the witnesses [as interpreted] passed through Deva on their way to Albania -- well, maybe through Deva or just close to it? I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I assume you're referring to the refugees?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. K89, we are talking about the refugees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It was on the way to Deva or adjacent to it. What if I told you that Deva is the last location that there are no other ways of reaching the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it is the last point, but we were closer to Zub. That road takes you somewhere, I don't know whether it ends at Deva.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So you say there is a road going further up. Is that towards the north?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether it stops at Deva or it passes by it close to the border post or to the left or to the right. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you participate in that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't tearing up any documents. It wasn't our position there. We were just patrolling there during day-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to provide short answers so as to be able to move as quickly as we can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Nobody from your unit was tearing up any documents. Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if anyone else participated, but I don't think anyone from my unit did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness K89, before this Chamber we heard a number of witnesses, as well as a number of witnesses who fled via that border post just below Zub. Not a single one of them stated that any army member tore up their documents; not a single Prosecution witness stated that, that the army was tearing up documents.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I saw people tearing up documents. I don't know what people did individually; however, there was tearing up of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you are not certain that this was done by the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army was there, the infantry. They were escorting them. I don't know why they were escorting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you know that there were minefields next to the road and that the soldiers were actually directing the civilians so as to avoid anyone being hurt in the minefields?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there were minefields, but where we were patrolling; and at our positions, there were none. I know that some of the other areas were mined.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the soldiers were trying to help the refugees, assist the infirm, and elderly, and they transported them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Soldiers even gave cookies and juices to children, whatever they had at hand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness K89. We can conclude, therefore, that the army behaved fairly towards the civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On average, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The witness cannot conclude on the conduct of the whole army. He can only say what he saw himself and how he saw people in this vision behave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. And he's also made it clear what he saw the soldiers doing, so it's for us to reach conclusions. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Then you mentioned houses being aflame. You stated who ordered you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My next question refers to the period before the 24th of March when you were at Zub. In your statement and during your testimony here, you said that when you were at Zub you targeted Smolice. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying that the range of the mortar you you're working with is 6.300 metres with the sixth charge and about five and a half kilometres with the fifth charge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying that you mostly used the fifth charge for firing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the average, five or six charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that Smolice is more than nine kilometres away from Zub as the crow flies, how can you explain the fact that you say you fired at Smolice from Zub?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we fired in the direction of Smolice. That's a village. I don't know. But that's what I heard, that Smolice was being targeted. I don't know whether it was into the centre of the village or a little before the village or beyond the village. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying that while you were at Zub, you had very little contact -- or, in fact, did you have any contact with civilians while you were at Zub?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not many contacts, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying that while you were at Zub - and that was before the start of the war - it was relatively quiet around your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part it was quiet. There was trouble at the border posts and you could hear that from a distance, but it didn't happen where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you see any refugees before the beginning of the NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How then do you explain the fact that an officer, whose name I will not repeat, ordered you on the 24th to tear up people's documents when there were no refugees at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 24th, NATO air-strikes began. The 25th, that is, there were no refugees there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: As I understood you, you did not see any refugees before the 24th, and you did not see any on the 24th and 25th either?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that I saw refugees; but then, when NATO began on the evening of the 24th, we didn't see any refugees. I did see some later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the basis for that question about an order to tear up people's documents? Was that in his evidence earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in his statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no. Is it in the evidence in this case, because for the moment I don't recollect this? He said the documents were torn up; that's not the issue. The issue is he being ordered to tear them up, because he's been quite clear so far that his unit didn't tear up any documents. It was other VJ units that he saw doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour, but in his statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I haven't got his statement, Mr. Visnjic, so there's no basis for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 3D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not being presented as part of the Prosecution evidence here --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: May I assist. I have a transcript reference where the witness first talked about the orders he received, and this is page 9124. And he said -- he told us that not a single Albanian ear was to remain in Kosovo and that their identification papers were to be torn so as to prevent them from coming back. He did not refer to refugees specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that conversation was when?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It's at the same transcript page. I asked him whether he received the specific order before he was redeployed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. What's the date, though, that he says this happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: We were talking about his redeployment to Orahovac, which was the 24th of March. In line 14 he says: "We were until the 24th of March when NATO begun its air-strikes." And then I asked: "At this point did you and other soldiers with you receive specific orders?" That's line 16. So this would be the time-frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's simply I haven't noted that particular part. I'm sorry about that, Mr. Visnjic. It's obviously my mistake. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Witness K89, bearing in mind what you testified about here, who could this order issued by your commanding officer refer to, if at that time there were no refugees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I couldn't really understand. The order was as it was. I don't know whether they knew that there would be refugees. I couldn't really get into his mind and --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that you remember correctly what he said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure. Perhaps I have missed -- I may have missed a couple of words. But I know that on the 25th, in the morning of the 25th, that was what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, your explanation is that they assumed that there would be refugees. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed that they assumed that because NATO carried out air-strikes and people were fleeing, probably not because of the army but because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I would like to know where the witness explained that they assumed that there would be refugees, and what -- the question is now asking him to speculate about what another person may have meant by saying something.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may respond, this is at this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not yet, please. Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes -- no, what is it you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that that is at page 62. I hope the transcript hasn't gone up. "I don't know whether they knew that there would be refugees."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. There's no objection to that question. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Witness K89, let us now move on to another topic. So my question to you was: "You assume that -- your explanation is that they assumed that there would be refugees. Am I right?" And your answer was not completed, so could you please complete it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably. I don't know what they thought, whether there would be some refugees. It is my opinion that there would be refugees, given that the NATO air-strikes and people would have to flee and take cover. I don't know what he may or may not have thought, but this is what I thought and probably this was what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Let us now go back to the incident where those people were killed and other uniform -- and uniforms were put on them. You explained to us that this happened in the vicinity of Orahovac. My question to you is whether you can describe in some detail the terrain in this area. Was there anything peculiar there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- nothing really sticks in my mind. I didn't -- don't remember the village. I can't really give you more details about where we were. It must have been to the left of Orahovac, I assume, but I'm not sure of that either. I'm not sure of the actual village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you see men being separated from the women and children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How long did this whole incident take?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how long it took precisely. I don't know whether the column came from this village or some other village. It was a refugee column, and then these people were separated. It didn't take long. At first I didn't know why they were separating them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This is a little bit confusing. Let me ask you this: How many people were there in this crowd from where people were being separated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I didn't count them. I don't know how many precisely. It was a large group of people, women, men, maybe 200. I don't know how many of them there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did all -- were all men separated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some men did remain in the big group. Whether they were the elderly people or whether they knew that they had taken part in something or whether they had some insignia identifying them as being part of the military, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How far away were you from the site of this incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That question has already been asked, and it's been answered before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Right, Your Honour, but I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it you're assuming that the remaining 15 minutes will be sufficient for everyone else's cross-examination, and the fact that you're going over something that has already been dealt with in cross-examination is a luxury you have the time to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will ask the following question then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't doubt that this is an important incident, but I don't think that really much thought has been given to how to deal with the cross-examination of this witness within the time available.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour, I will try to do it on shorter way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may not be your fault. I'm just wanting you to make sure you're conscious of everyone's interests in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D495. That's a Defence exhibit. Can it just be at stand-by. We don't need to show it to the witness yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Witness K89, that you remained in the Orahovac area from the 25th of March until the 2nd of April, 1999, which would be a total of nine days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you remained in the Orahovac area, that you were there with two trucks. In addition to the crews, those trucks were used to transport the equipment and the weapons for the mortars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three trucks or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is it true that while you were in the Orahovac area, that you operated as a support unit and that you did not open fire because there were no requests from the battalion commander or the units that you provided support to, to that effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did not open fire, but we went about in order to be with those units, in order to be able to provide support.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to move into private session now, and I would like the witness to be shown Defence Exhibit 3D495, page 7.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You've told us about firing your mortars in the direction of the village of Smolice; and at one point your, commander mentioned to you that you had actually targeted a mosque there. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And another thing that you were given to understand was that Smolice was a KLA stronghold and that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: -- you were told that that mosque was being used as a sniper post, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now, did you ever actually go to Smolice and see that village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not into the village itself actually. We went to fetch water with a tank nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you see the village? Could you tell whether or not there was a mosque there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I saw it, you couldn't see a mosque. It would have been already destroyed if it had been the target, as the commander said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could it be possible that Smolice is a Catholic village and it had no mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now, one thing that I'm just curious about in your statement, and it could be an error of some sort. But in paragraph 22 of your statement, you talk about driving from Sulani to Zub. And you talk about driving for five or six hours to get from Sulani to Zub. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't that far. It was five or six kilometres. I wasn't talking about hours. There may be an error here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That's clearly the case. Thank you. This shelling by mortar, this shooting by mortar, in the direction of this village of Smolice, that went on for four or five months, did it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when we went to Sulani. We didn't do much firing. The firing was when we were at -- was before. We would have a day off. It was gone for a few days. It would all depend on the situation and on the support the infantry needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But this -- this business of firing on Smolice and assisting the infantry with regard to Smolice, I think you said went on for four or five months. Isn't that the case, off and on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it did last a long time. We were at the positions for a long time. Most of the time was at -- at Kosovo was at Sulani, Zub. We stayed at Zub for three, four, five months, or at Sulani we could have been for four months. And those were the positions we held.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: All right. I want to go on to something else now. In paragraph 32 of your statement you -- you're talking about near the end when you're getting ready to withdraw. You said: "When we eventually withdrew, some people wanted to burn the villages." Now, when you say "some people wanted to burn the villages," what people are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know their names. We had a shed of sorts, and we had to cover our tracks and burn it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, you're not one of the people that wanted to burn house as you were withdrawing, are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't want to do that. About ten days before the withdrawal, I had orders. I didn't want to set fire to houses, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In fact, you told us about being issued an order at one point to burn a house, and you didn't carry out that order. After the person who had issued had left, your commander did not require you to follow that order, did he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now, when you say these people wanted to burn the villages, the officers that were with you at that point wouldn't permit that to happen, would they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our commander wouldn't permit it, and we ourselves didn't want to do it. There were NATO forces. We were just an escort. We didn't even try to set fire to anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In your statement during your supplementary visit with the Prosecutor, you said this: "During the bombing, soldiers, mostly reserve units, were often drunk when going through villages looting. They were not in close contact with the officers and, therefore, became slack in their discipline and appearance." I take it it's your view that if they had been in close contact with the officers, the officers would have prevented this from happening; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And just one final question. You talk about some things you've observed; these shootings that you observed and the tearing of documents that you observed.
