Did you actually make any reports of these observations to your higher officers and tell them what you had seen so that they would deal with it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't personally make any reports because it wasn't done by someone from my company. If it had been, I might have reported it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One thing I didn't understand there in your evidence. You said that your commander wouldn't permit the burning of villages. "We ourselves didn't want to do it. There were NATO forces. We were just an escort." What did you mean that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if I was very precise in my answer. (redacted), did not allow us to burn or loot; and had we wanted to do so, had any of our soldiers wanted to do so, we did not dare. We couldn't have done it because we were under escort. We had helicopter and aeroplane surveillance all the way as we pulled out towards Serbia, as we pulled out from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila and Mr. O'Sullivan have no questions. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. K89. My name is Branko Lukic, and I will just try to clarify a few points with you. You gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 23rd of January, 2006. This statement was read out to you in a language you understand, and you signed it as being accurate. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 27 of this statement, you speak about a unit or a group of people that you were told were Arkan's Tigers and you describe them as follows. "These groups -- there were also groups that I was told were from Arkan's Tigers. These groups wore blue berets and a different sort of uniform. Rather than the regular uniform that we wore, these other groups wore one-piece boiler suits. They were all green camouflage but different shades of green." Those shades of green, were they lighter or darker than the uniforms you wore?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were a bit lighter than our uniforms. They were not the same as our uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it was green but lighter than your uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were like blue, but there were also some shades of green. They were lighter in colour than the camouflage uniforms that we wore, because they also had this boiler suit-type uniforms with a jacket worn over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any direct contacts with them, or did you base your knowledge that those were Arkan's Tigers on what other people told you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no direct contacts with them. A colleague of mine told me -- I asked, "Why are they wearing this -- these uniforms?" And he said, "Those are Arkan's Tigers." That's what they were called. Perhaps those were soldiers that were better dressed than we rank-and-file soldiers, but that's what he told me. That's how I knew that those were those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters did not get the question because the microphone was not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to apologise. I have to ask you this question again because I had turned off my microphone. You don't know who was their commander, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Ms. Moeller, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, I do have some questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that will have to be after lunchtime. We need another break, K89, and the usher will take you from the court in a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The transcript, I hope, should reflect what I actually said that she has to deal with a very urgent personal matter. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Re-examination by Ms. Moeller

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Witness K89, Mr. Cepic at the beginning of the cross-examination asked you about whether the soldiers could or would go to town once a week during their national military service. Now, in 1999, after the 24th of March while you were in the Orahovac area, could you actually do that, go to town once a week?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say, the question is not quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall Mr. Cepic asking you whether during your military training soldiers would go to town once a week?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's when he was in Valjevo, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I think it wasn't specified. It's transcript page 23, line 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I've noted in my note that it related to Valjevo, but I may be wrong. Which page did you say it was? 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: 23 and line -- page 23, line 21. Okay. Yes. I'm sorry, Your Honour. Yes, it says "Valjevo." I withdraw the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Cepic also talked about 20 criminal reports that were filed with regard to the units you were deployed in. Now, during your time in Kosovo in 1999, did you ever see any soldier or any other person in the field being disciplined or punished or taken out of any combat operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not see or hear about anyone being punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cepic also asked you about -- he showed you a document 5D87, and he asked you about the 24th or 25th of March and your deployment to Orahovac. Now, can you clarify, as that wasn't really clear, who went at that time to Orahovac. Was it the whole company or was it part?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the whole company, but just the 1st Platoon in the company that had two mortars. The rest of the company remained in the positions that we had been occupying before. So it was not the entire company that left, less than half, one-third of the company in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then Mr. Cepic also talked with you about the convoy that you saw passing by Deva, and he mentioned minefields being there and asked you whether you knew about them. Now, do you know whether there were any minefields close to where this convoy was passing by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the location where we were, I didn't know whether there were any minefields. But -- but we -- if it had been -- if there had been minefields, we wouldn't have been able to move about. But I think maybe along the border there were some mines laid, but in the area where we were there were no mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also told Mr. Cepic that the infirm and elderly in this convoy were transported by the VJ on vehicles. Which direction were they taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were taken further up from the position where we were. I don't know whether they were taken right to the border or perhaps somewhere else, but we were at Zub. I don't know whether they were taken to Deva, because that was in the direction that they were being taken. Whether they were left off at Deva or whether they were taken even further away from there, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then there was some discussion about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you go on with that question, just let the record reflect that Judge Kamenova has now joined the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic also asked you about the firing of charges with the mortar, and that wasn't quite clear to me. It's transcript page 59, lines 14 to page 60. He asked you whether it was correct that you were working mainly with the sixth charge and the fifth charge, and you said, "It's possible." And then you said -- he asked: "Would I be correct in saying that you mostly used the fifth charge for firing?" And you responded: "Well, on average, five or six charges." Would you explain to us what relation, if any, exists between these charges and the distance you're firing at.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a difference. I don't know what actually affects the range, whether this depends on the shell; but, in fact, the most important part of the shell would be the charge. A lot of things affect the range. If you have a charge five or five charges then your range is less than if you have six, but the shells were the same. So I think the charges are the most important thing, but I did not really have time to learn about this. I didn't undergo any training anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, during 1998 in the villages of Sulani and Zub, were there any Kosovo Albanian civilians in these villages while the army was in this area, too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K89 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. While we were at Sulani, there weren't any near to us; but when we went down to get some water, there were civilians there. There were no problems there, in fact. Everything just went as normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I have some last questions which I would like to lead in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution's next scheduled witness is K90, K-9-0. Your Honour, I've sent an e-mail earlier this morning I think to your Legal Officer and to the Defence. I'm requesting, if Your Honours will grant my request, that he begin his evidence on Monday morning. You're aware, Your Honours, of some of the difficulties we've had in getting this witness to attend. He arrived in The Hague yesterday sometime in the afternoon. I don't know what time he arrived here. He was scheduled to appear at our office this morning at 9.30 for proofing. When victims witnesses went to pick him up at the hotel, he refused to come and says he hadn't slept or eaten for two days. I don't know the particulars of that. They didn't want to try and physically bring him to my office. We've had his statement and we agreed to meet him tomorrow morning. I. Have not met him we have had numerous discussions with him over the past two or three months and my investigators have, but those they have been dealing with logistics; with him coming here, talking about the subpoena, talking about protective measures, talking about his reluctance to appear. And I have not met him. I have not had one word with him. In his statement, in the penultimate paragraph - I think I mentioned that in the e-mail as well - he indicated he had seen and knew of other incidents in Kosovo that he was willing to talk about. That's one thing I wanted to explore with him. And I feel there will - assuming he shows up tomorrow and actually speaks with me, and doesn't fold his arms and refuse to speak - there will be a supplemental information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the date of that, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Nobody thought about trying to investigate it between 2002 and now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I don't know the answer. I think we assume -- I know when we selected him for the witness list, reading the statement, we thought that this would be -- we didn't have any reason at that time to believe that he wasn't going to come --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. No, I'm concerned about the additional information he may have to provide. If nobody knows whether it's been investigated -- rather, if anybody should know if it's been investigated, it must be you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want him for the evidence he's already told us about in the statement; and, certainly, I expect that's the most significant and most pertinent to our case. But based on other statements sometimes when witnesses say they have to lot to tell, they really have not much at all. And sometimes they actually do have things that are more significant than anything they did say. I just don't know. My estimated time for him, Your Honour, was three hours on direct. So even if we brought him in cold tomorrow without having speaking with him, there's a chance if I took three hours and Defence took three hours we would go into next week. I understand the Prosecution may incur a penalty for loss of time on Friday, but I think it will be a smoother presentation if we proceed this way. I can get the supplemental information over to the Defence and have that prepared for them to digest for whatever it may raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic, is there anything to be said by the Defence about this suggestion that you have Friday off.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We'll welcome that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it that's strenuously opposed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What it would do, of course, would present you with a golden opportunity to do some work on your agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid that Mr. Hannis will be proofing the witness, so therefore I don't see -- we will definitely try, Your Honours, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sure he's not the only person who can deal with that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But I would expect him to be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- you've recognised what's the possible consequence of this. The clock is running. Exactly how it's going to be taken into account we've already indicated at an earlier occasion will be determined at a later stage. There may come a point when we actually apply a sanction. At the moment we simply give the yellow card warning that it's running, and you can take it that some regard will be had to this loss of time in due course and possibly to others. However, we will grant the motion to adjourn until Monday. And on Monday we sit at 9.00 I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I may be pushing my luck, but I have one other request I wanted to make. I indicated to you I would file my written submissions concerning the additional exhibits pertaining to General Vasiljevic. I would like to ask your permission to extend that to Monday as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, that's in order in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The redactions that you've asked about have been dealt with meanwhile and an appropriate order has been signed -- or a number of orders have been signed to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll resume at 9.00 on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
